neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Oriented to person and place; disoriented to date. Slow speech. Asterixis absent on standard exam. Asterixis present on prolonged arm extension (90 seconds). Mild incoordination noted.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, reactive. Mild ophthalmoparesis — limited upward gaze and abduction bilaterally. Nystagmus on lateral gaze. Facial symmetry intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral upper extremity weakness 4/5. Ataxic-type movements.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased vibration sensation bilateral feet and ankles. Absent Romberg test — significant sway.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs absent bilateral lower extremities. DTRs 1+ upper extremities.
neurological_exam.coordination: Moderate dysmetria on finger-nose. Gait ataxia.
neurological_exam.gait: Severely ataxic — unable to walk without assistance. Positive Romberg.
neurological_exam.additional: The combination of ophthalmoparesis, nystagmus, ataxia, and confusion in a nutritionally deficient patient with celiac disease and cirrhosis raises the possibility of Wernicke encephalopathy, NOT just HE. Celiac disease with malabsorption causes thiamine deficiency even without alcohol use. Recent gastrointestinal illness with vomiting x 7 days before admission.

patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities in NASH cirrhosis patient with celiac disease — HE vs Wernicke encephalopathy
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. P. is a 49-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism who presents after 7 days of severe vomiting and poor oral intake from a gastrointestinal illness. She is brought by a friend who found her ataxic, confused, and unable to walk. On exam, she has ophthalmoparesis (limited upward gaze and bilateral abduction), nystagmus on lateral gaze, truncal and appendicular ataxia, absent lower extremity reflexes, decreased vibration sensation in feet, and confusion with asterixis on prolonged arm extension. Her ammonia is 68 µmol/L — mildly elevated. She has BOTH hepatic encephalopathy risk factors (NASH cirrhosis, MELD 13, prior HE) AND severe Wernicke encephalopathy risk factors (celiac disease malabsorption of thiamine, 7 days of vomiting/poor intake, nutritional deficiency, non-alcoholic Wernicke). This is a critical puzzle: (1) HE and Wernicke can coexist and both cause confusion; (2) the ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus are NEVER features of HE — they point to Wernicke; (3) missing Wernicke and treating only HE risks irreversible neurological injury; (4) thiamine MUST be given before glucose in this patient regardless of which diagnosis is primary.

eeg.impression: The EEG cannot distinguish between the two. The clinical syndrome (ophthalmoparesis + nystagmus + ataxia) and thiamine level (24 nmol/L) are diagnostic for Wernicke — the EEG is supportive but non-specific. Clinical correlation recommended.

ct.impression: CT head normal. Wernicke encephalopathy CANNOT be excluded on CT — requires MRI. Structural hemorrhage excluded.
recommended_actions: Do NOT delay thiamine while waiting for MRI — treat empirically NOW

Thiamine_Treatment.test: Thiamine IV 500 mg TID x 3 days (URGENT — Wernicke protocol)

Thiamine_Treatment.value: Partial improvement — vertical gaze improving; nystagmus reduced
Thiamine_Treatment.reference_range: Wernicke ocular signs respond within hours to days

abnormal_values_summary: Thiamine normalized; ophthalmoparesis improving — Wernicke diagnosis confirmed by treatment response

output.modality: MRI Brain with and without gadolinium
output.indication: Wernicke encephalopathy — confirm periaqueductal and mammillary body T2 signal

findings.description: BILATERAL T2/FLAIR HYPERINTENSITY IN PERIAQUEDUCTAL GRAY MATTER — classic Wernicke finding
Bilateral mammillary body T2 hyperintensity with enhancement post-gadolinium — pathognomonic for Wernicke encephalopathy
Bilateral medial thalami T2 signal — additional Wernicke-associated location
Mild T1 hyperintensity bilateral globus pallidi — manganese from cirrhosis
No DWI restriction in cortex (acute infarct excluded)

output.impression: MRI confirms WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY: periaqueductal gray matter + mammillary body T2 signal with enhancement — these are pathognomonic locations for thiamine deficiency. The MRI finding combined with clinical triad (ophthalmoparesis, ataxia, confusion) and thiamine level 24 nmol/L is definitive.
recommended_actions: Wernicke encephalopathy definitively confirmed by MRI
Continue high-dose IV thiamine 500 mg TID for 5 days
Transition to oral thiamine 100 mg TID after IV course
Treat concurrent HE with lactulose + rifaximin

output.proposed: Optimize nutritional replacement in celiac disease with cirrhosis
interactions: Celiac disease malabsorption affects: thiamine, folate, B12, iron, calcium, magnesium, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
Strict gluten-free diet improves intestinal absorption but does not immediately reverse nutritional deficiencies
Calcium carbonate absorption requires stomach acid — use calcium citrate if on acid suppression
contraindications: Calcium carbonate if on PPI — use calcium citrate instead (better absorbed without acid)
warnings: Thiamine malabsorption in celiac is underappreciated — non-alcoholic Wernicke in celiac is a real risk
Vitamin K deficiency from celiac malabsorption may worsen INR in cirrhosis
alternatives: Daily oral thiamine 100 mg lifelong for celiac + cirrhosis
Monthly IM B12 injections if oral absorption unreliable

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy + hepatic encephalopathy — in NASH cirrhosis patient with celiac disease malabsorption; 7 days of vomiting causes thiamine depletion (24 nmol/L); ophthalmoparesis, nystagmus, and ataxia = Wernicke (not HE); MRI confirms periaqueductal and mammillary body signal

differential.key_features: Ophthalmoparesis + nystagmus + ataxia + confusion in nutritionally deficient patient = Wernicke; BUT ammonia 68 with cirrhosis confirms concurrent HE; both diagnoses are present simultaneously
HE does NOT cause ophthalmoparesis or nystagmus — eye movement abnormalities are incompatible with HE; the presence of these findings mandates Wernicke workup and thiamine treatment
Celiac neuropathy causes peripheral and cerebellar ataxia; however, the acute presentation with ophthalmoparesis and very low thiamine points to Wernicke, not slow celiac neurodegeneration

MFS causes ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia — but no antecedent infection; liver disease present; thiamine deficient; LFTs abnormal; MFS is seronegative; Wernicke is far more likely in this context

optimal_actions.action: URGENT: IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE any dextrose — severely deficient thiamine (24 nmol/L), celiac malabsorption + 7 days vomiting, non-alcoholic Wernicke
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Thiamine administered; ophthalmoparesis begins to improve within hours

optimal_actions.action: IV Magnesium sulfate — hypomagnesemia prevents thiamine activation
Labs — thiamine, ammonia, Mg, K, Na, LFTs, folate, B12
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Thiamine 24 (severely deficient), Mg 1.3, ammonia 68 — dual diagnosis confirmed

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain urgently — confirm Wernicke (periaqueductal + mammillary body T2)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: CT normal — no hemorrhage; MRI required for Wernicke confirmation

optimal_actions.action: EEG — characterize encephalopathy; lactulose + rifaximin for HE component
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Non-specific theta slowing — HE + Wernicke both present

critical_actions: Ophthalmoparesis + nystagmus is INCOMPATIBLE with hepatic encephalopathy alone — these findings mandate Wernicke workup and empiric IV thiamine IMMEDIATELY
Hypomagnesemia must be corrected WITH thiamine — Mg is required for thiamine pyrophosphate (active form); thiamine without Mg correction is less effective
Non-alcoholic Wernicke (from celiac malabsorption) is underrecognized — Wernicke is not exclusive to alcoholics; celiac, cancer, prolonged vomiting, bariatric surgery all cause Wernicke
IV thiamine must be given at HIGH dose (500 mg TID) for established Wernicke — standard prophylactic doses (100-200 mg) are insufficient for treatment of established disease
contraindicated_actions: Any dextrose before thiamine — risks precipitating/worsening Wernicke by consuming the remaining thiamine for glucose metabolism
Treating only HE and missing Wernicke — Korsakoff syndrome (permanent amnesia) results from untreated Wernicke
Low-dose thiamine (100 mg) for established Wernicke — treatment requires 500 mg TID IV
key_reasoning_points: Ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus = Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise in a nutritionally deficient patient — these are NEVER features of HE
Wernicke encephalopathy occurs in non-alcoholics — celiac disease, cancer cachexia, prolonged vomiting, post-bariatric surgery, and hyperemesis gravidarum are all recognized causes
Hypomagnesemia blocks thiamine activation — correcting Mg simultaneously with thiamine is essential for full treatment effect
HE and Wernicke can coexist — both require simultaneous treatment; treating only one will result in partial recovery and risk permanent Korsakoff neurological injury

red_herrings.data_point: NASH cirrhosis with prior HE + ammonia 68 µmol/L
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all confusion to HE; initiate lactulose + rifaximin; miss Wernicke encephalopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus are NOT features of HE — their presence demands Wernicke evaluation and immediate IV thiamine; missing Wernicke leads to Korsakoff syndrome

red_herrings.intended_effect: Focus on celiac neuropathy or gluten ataxia as cause of cerebellar findings; initiate gluten-free diet adjustment; miss Wernicke
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: While celiac can cause cerebellar ataxia (gluten ataxia), the ACUTE presentation with ophthalmoparesis, severely low thiamine (24 nmol/L), and 7 days of vomiting points to Wernicke as the acute precipitant — treat Wernicke immediately, then optimize celiac management long-term

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy (non-alcoholic, from celiac malabsorption + vomiting) and HE; ophthalmoparesis/nystagmus are Wernicke signs incompatible with HE; hypomagnesemia blocks thiamine; MRI confirms periaqueductal + mammillary body signal
